opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, incredibly useful. I mean, clearly people have been able to take care of babies without ChatGPT for a very long time, so I don't know how I would have done that otherwise, but I leaned on it constantly, especially in those first few weeks. It was a lot of very basic questions at two in the morning: is this normal, why is he doing this, how much should he be eating, that kind of thing.

And then over time it shifted more toward developmental stages, like what should I expect at this point, what's typical, what's worth paying attention to. It's kind of become this always-available person I can ask anything, without feeling silly about asking the same thing for the fifth time.

The other thing that struck me is that it made me think a lot about the world my kid is going to grow up in. He's never going to know a world where computers aren't smarter than him in a lot of ways, and to him that'll just be completely normal, the way touchscreens were normal to kids a decade ago. That's a strange thing to sit with as a parent, but mostly I find it exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says his questions shifted from basic newborn concerns to developmental stages, but it does not connect that shift to growing competence at basic baby care.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot more than I expected. In those first few weeks I was using it constantly. I don't know how people did it before, I mean obviously they did, people have raised kids forever, but it's the middle of the night, the baby is making some noise you've never heard before, and you want to know if this is normal or if you should be worried. Being able to just ask, in plain language, and get a calm, reasonable answer right then was really valuable. It didn't replace the pediatrician, and I don't think it should, but it was there at 3 a.m. when the pediatrician wasn't.

The thing that surprised me was how much it helped with the small, dumb stuff too. Like, what's a reasonable nap schedule at this age, or why is he doing this weird thing with his hands. And then over time it got less about panic and more about curiosity. You start asking about developmental stages, what to expect in the next couple months, how to think about introducing foods.

I'll also say it made me think a lot about what it's going to be like for him. He's never going to know a world where these tools don't exist. That's a strange thing to sit with as a parent. Mostly I think it's good. He'll have this incredibly patient thing that can explain anything to him at whatever level he's at. But it does make me want to get the details right.

r001.rationale: The response says questions shifted from panic to curiosity and included developmental stages, but it does not link that shift to Sam becoming more competent at basic baby care.

astra-6.text: It’s been really useful for the little questions that come up constantly as a new parent. You’re tired, something’s unfamiliar, and you want help thinking through what to ask or what to pay attention to. It doesn’t replace a pediatrician, but having something available at three in the morning that can explain things calmly is pretty valuable.
